# 2. Insert breakpoint() (Python 3.7+) to drop into pdb, then use `p variable`, `l`, and `n` to inspect live state step by step.

# 5. Print repr(value) instead of value to expose hidden whitespace, control characters, or type differences that str() silently masks.
# 6. Guard assumptions with assert statements (e.g., assert isinstance(x, int)) so invariant violations fail loudly at the exact spot they occur.
# 7. Use f-string self-documenting output like print(f"{data=}") to dump variable names alongside values while tracing flow through a function.
# 8. Bisect the failure: use git bisect or comment out half the code to narrow which commit or block introduced the misbehavior.
# 9. Diff expected versus actual output side by side instead of eyeballing, since tiny discrepancies hide easily in long or similar-looking text.
# 10. Stub out I/O, network calls, and randomness with fixed values so behavior becomes deterministic and the bug repeats on every run.

requests.content:
1. # Reproduce the bug deterministically first: pin inputs, seed random state, and freeze time so the failure occurs on every run.
2. # Read the full traceback from the bottom up: the last "File ..., line N" frame usually points at the code that actually raised.
3. # Log variable values at branch points (logger.debug(f"x={x!r}, state={state!r}")) instead of guessing what the runtime state is.
4. # Drop breakpoint() into the suspect function and inspect locals with pdb commands like p, pp, and up before changing any code.
5. # Bisect the failure: comment out half the suspect code (or use git bisect on commits) to halve the search space each iteration.
6. # Print type(x) and repr(x) at data boundaries — most crashes come from values being a different type or shape than assumed (None, empty list, str vs bytes).
7. # Write a failing test that reproduces the bug before fixing it, then keep it as a regression test so the fix is proven and locked in.
8. # Check boundary conditions explicitly: off-by-one at loop edges, empty collections, first/last elements, and zero or negative inputs.
9. # Explain the code aloud line by line (rubber-duck debugging); the mismatch between what you say it does and what it does usually exposes the bug.
10. # Diff against a known-good version: compare current output, logs, or git diff with the last working state to spot exactly what changed.
